summary: This Standards Track document adds post-quantum public key algorithms to OpenPGP, extending RFC 9580. It defines composite encryption based on ML-KEM and composite signatures based on ML-DSA, aiming at long-term secure signatures and ciphertexts.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives your secret-message program new locks built to withstand future super-computers, paired with the old ones.

questions: what is post-quantum cryptography in openpgp
which openpgp algorithm ids are post-quantum
subtitle: New OpenPGP key types that pair post-quantum algorithms with elliptic curves, so a future quantum computer cannot read or forge the traffic.

tldr.problem: OpenPGP keys rely on factoring and discrete logarithm problems, which a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) could break.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9980 adds ML-KEM + X25519/X448 composite encryption, ML-DSA + EdDSA composite signatures, and standalone SLH-DSA signatures as new OpenPGP public key algorithms (IDs 30 to 36).
tldr.outcome: OpenPGP implementations get interoperable post-quantum keys that keep working if either half of a composite pair is broken. It extends RFC 9580 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9980 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026 and is not marked as obsoleted or updated, so it is the current definition of post-quantum algorithms in OpenPGP. It extends RFC 9580.

sections.title: Why Post-Quantum OpenPGP
sections.content:
OpenPGP, defined in RFC 9580, supports public key algorithms based on the factoring or discrete logarithm problem. These are endangered by quantum computers, so RFC 9980 extends OpenPGP with algorithms that stay secure against a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC): a quantum computer able to break traditional public key cryptography.

The algorithms come from the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization process, which NIST began in 2016 and which chose algorithms in mid-2022. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM), a modern building block for public key encryption. ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are signature schemes.

ML-KEM and ML-DSA are used conservatively, in combination with traditional schemes, so security is kept even if all but one of the combined schemes are broken. These combinations are called multi-algorithm or post-quantum/traditional (PQ/T) hybrids. SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based scheme whose security assumptions are considered well enough understood to use on its own. The text uses composite to mean that a combination appears as a single data structure or algorithm from the protocol's point of view.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's locks might one day be picked by a super-powerful new kind of computer. So this document adds new locks, and for the two main ones it keeps the old lock on the door as a backup.

sections.title: The New Algorithms and What Is Required
sections.content:
Seven new public key algorithm IDs are defined, and each is fully specified by its ID, with no parameters. For signatures: 30 (ML-DSA-65+Ed25519), 31 (ML-DSA-87+Ed448), 32 (SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s), 33 (SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f) and 34 (SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s). For encryption: 35 (ML-KEM-768+X25519) and 36 (ML-KEM-1024+X448).

A conformant implementation MUST implement ML-DSA-65+Ed25519 and ML-KEM-768+X25519. It SHOULD also implement ML-DSA-87+Ed448 and ML-KEM-1024+X448, though it may omit them in a highly constrained environment. Any of the SLH-DSA algorithms is a MAY.

The two ID pairs give two security levels as a trade-off with performance. For SLH-DSA, the "128f" variant is faster at signing and "128s" gives smaller signatures. For SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256, only the small variant is offered, to contain signature size.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a menu of new locks, with a small, medium and fancy size. Every program has to be able to use the standard one, and the fancier ones are strongly suggested.

sections.title: How Algorithms Combine
sections.content:
In a composite KEM, ML-KEM and an ECDH KEM are used together in an inseparable way. Both encapsulations or decapsulations run in parallel, and the two resulting key shares feed a key combiner that outputs one shared secret. A composite signature is an independent ML-DSA signature and EdDSA signature, and an implementation MUST validate both to call it valid.

OpenPGP also allows a message to carry several signatures, and to be encrypted to several keys. An implementation MAY sign with both a traditional key and a PQ(/T) key, so a legacy implementation can fall back on the traditional signature. Newer implementations MAY ignore traditional signatures and SHOULD consider the message correctly signed if at least one non-ignored signature validates. Encrypting a message to several keys is not post-quantum secure unless all of those keys use PQ(/T) encryption schemes.

Two further rules apply. The zero point (point at infinity) MUST NOT appear in any ECC data structure defined here. And all PQ(/T) algorithms are for v6 (and newer) keys and certificates, with one exception: ML-KEM-768+X25519 (ID 35) is also allowed in v4 encryption-capable subkeys.
sections.plainLanguage: For the main new locks, your door has two locks at once, and a visitor must open both. If someone later learns to pick one, the other still holds.

sections.title: Composite Encryption with ML-KEM
sections.content:
To encrypt a session key to a composite recipient key, the sender first takes the ECDH and ML-KEM public keys out of the recipient's key packet. It then runs the ECDH KEM (X25519-KEM or X448-KEM) and ML-KEM encapsulation, which give an ECDH ciphertext and key share and an ML-KEM ciphertext and key share.

A key combiner turns these into a Key Encryption Key (KEK) using SHA3-256 over the ML-KEM key share, the ECDH key share, the ECDH ciphertext, the ECDH public key, the algorithm ID, a domain-separation constant and its length. The constant domSep is the UTF-8 string OpenPGPCompositeKDFv1, and its length octet is decimal 21. The construction follows the QSF/X-Wing design.

The session key is then wrapped with AES-256 Key Wrap as in RFC 3394, using the KEK, which includes a 64-bit integrity check. The recipient reverses the steps: decapsulates both KEMs, recomputes the KEK, unwraps the key, and aborts if the integrity check fails. The key generation rule is that the ML-KEM and ECDH component keys MUST be generated independently.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender mixes two secret ingredients, one from each lock, into a single key. That key then locks up the message key inside a box that only the recipient can open.

sections.title: Packet Layouts for Encryption Keys
sections.content:
The algorithm-specific part of a Public Key Encrypted Session Key (PKESK) packet is, in order: the ECDH ephemeral public key, the ML-KEM ciphertext, a one-octet length of what follows, a one-octet symmetric algorithm ID (only in a v3 PKESK), and the wrapped session key. In a v3 PKESK, that symmetric algorithm ID is sent in plaintext and MUST be AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256 (IDs 7, 8 or 9). The receiver MUST check that the unwrapped key length matches that algorithm.

The public key packet holds the ECC public key followed by the ML-KEM public key. The secret key packet holds the ECDH secret key followed by the ML-KEM secret key in seed format, which is 64 octets made of the values d and z, 32 octets each. Implementations MUST NOT use the obsolete Symmetrically Encrypted Data packet (Packet Type ID 9) with these algorithms.

ID 35 may be used with v4 or v6 keys, and ID 36 only with v6 keys.
sections.plainLanguage: This section is the packing list for the parcel: which pieces go in the box, in what order, and how big each piece is.

sections.title: Composite Signatures with ML-DSA
sections.content:
To sign, the signer builds the data digest as in RFC 9580, creates an EdDSA signature and an ML-DSA signature over that digest, and encodes both into the signature packet. To verify, both signatures are checked and both must pass. "EdDSA" here means PureEdDSA from RFC 8032, and "ML-DSA" means the default hedged version from FIPS 204. Both use an empty context string.

These schemes are for v6 signatures and v6 keys only. The signature packet holds the EdDSA signature followed by the ML-DSA signature. A composite signature MUST use a hash algorithm with a digest size of at least 256 bits, and a verifier MUST reject anything smaller.

The ML-DSA secret key is stored as a 32-octet seed. The two component keys MUST be generated independently.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature here is two signatures stapled together, one old style and one new style. The signature only counts if both are real.

sections.title: Standalone SLH-DSA Signatures
sections.content:
SLH-DSA is defined as a standalone signature scheme, with no traditional partner, because its security rests only on the hardness of finding preimages for hash functions. Three parameter sets are provided: SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s (ID 32), SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f (ID 33) and SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s (ID 34). Keys and signatures are fixed-length octet strings, listed in the table below.

As with ML-DSA, SLH-DSA uses the default hedged signing, an empty context string, v6 signatures and v6 keys only, and a hash digest size of at least 256 bits, with verifiers rejecting smaller ones.
sections.plainLanguage: This lock uses a completely different trick, so it travels alone. Its downside is that its signature stamps are quite big.

sections.title: Migration and Compatibility
sections.content:
Not every client will support the new algorithms during the transition, so the RFC offers guidance. When encrypting, an implementation MAY by default encrypt to both PQ(/T) and traditional keys of a recipient to avoid disruption, optionally showing a warning. This is not post-quantum secure unless every PKESK uses a PQ(/T) scheme.

When signing, signing with only PQ(/T) key material is not backwards compatible. When verifying, an implementation MAY accept both kinds, and a verifier worried about a CRQC that knows a peer has a PQ(/T) signing key MAY ignore that peer's traditional signatures.

When generating PQ(/T) keys, it is RECOMMENDED to create fresh secrets. Reusing material from existing ECC keys gives no backwards compatibility.

Implementations MUST implement AES-256, and SHOULD use AES-256 (with an AEAD mode for v2 SEIPD) when all recipient certificates indicate support. Certificates with a PQ(/T) key SHOULD list AES-256 and the AES-256 with OCB pair in their preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Some friends still have only the old locks. So for a while you can use both old and new locks on a message, knowing the old lock alone is not future-proof.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The composite signatures are not subject to signature stripping. The hashed metadata of every OpenPGP signature includes the signature algorithm ID, so a component signature taken out of its composite is not a valid signature for any message. Remixing parts of two composite signatures also fails because each v6 signature embeds a random salt at the start of its hashed metadata.

The key combiner is argued to be IND-CCA2-secure if ML-KEM is IND-CCA2-secure or the Strong Diffie-Hellman problem holds in a nominal group, which Curve25519 and Curve448 qualify as. Including the ECC public key also covers multi-target attacks. The domain-separation string and length octet prevent collisions across domains, and the algorithm ID binds the KEK to the chosen algorithm.

The hedged variants of ML-DSA and SLH-DSA mix fresh randomness into signing for better side-channel resistance. Because v6 signatures include a leading random salt, the required hash property is second-preimage resistance, so a 256-bit digest suffices. Empty context strings are used for interoperability, so the RFC recommends avoiding key reuse across protocols to prevent cross-protocol attacks. All random data must come from a CSPRNG.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors checked that nobody can peel one lock off, mix pieces from two signed messages, or reuse a key in a trick. They also say to always use truly random numbers.

sections.title: Performance Trade-offs for SLH-DSA
sections.content:
ML-DSA + EdDSA runs at a speed close to traditional ECC signatures, though ML-DSA has far larger signatures and public keys than ECC or even RSA. SLH-DSA relies on weaker assumptions, namely only the second-preimage resistance of a hash function, which may give more trust in long-term signatures. But its signatures are larger and its signing is slower than ML-DSA + EdDSA.

Depending on the parameter set, SLH-DSA signature generation takes approximately one hundred to more than two thousand times as long as ML-DSA-87. Choose SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128f for fast signing, SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s for the smallest signature (about double the size of an ML-DSA-87 signature), and SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256s when more than 128 bits of security are needed. Verification is closer: larger than ML-DSA-87 by a factor of four for -128s, nine for -256s and twelve for -128f.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra-safe lock is slow to make and its stamp is big. You can pick a quicker lock with a bigger stamp, or a slower one with a smaller stamp.

data.title: multiKeyCombine
data.code:
KEK = SHA3-256(
    mlkemKeyShare || ecdhKeyShare ||
    ecdhCipherText || ecdhPublicKey ||
    algId || domSep || len(domSep)
)
